claims.text: FeCuCrCoNi HEA nanoparticles have a size-dependent thermal response.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have lower thermal stability under heating than larger particles.
Enhanced surface disorder and modified short-range ordering cause the lower thermal stability of smaller particles.
The nanoparticles can be initialized as disordered random solid solutions.
Molecular dynamics simulations with systematic variation of nanoparticle size and controlled heating can be used to study the thermal response.
Temperatures from approximately room temperature to 1000 K are suitable simulation conditions.
Embedded-atom-method interatomic potentials are appropriate for these FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticle simulations.
Nanosecond-scale simulations can be used to investigate the proposed thermal response.
Smaller nanoparticles have stronger surface effects because of their greater surface-to-volume ratio.
Stronger surface effects in smaller FeCuCrCoNi particles produce greater atomic displacement.
A larger fraction of atoms at or near the surface promotes increased atomic mobility and disorder under thermal stress.
Changes in chemical short-range order affect lattice thermal conductivity and atomic displacement.
In smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles, changes in short-range order adversely affect thermal transport by increasing atomic displacement.
Size-dependent short-range ordering alters the vibrational density of states.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will exhibit increased atomic displacement, less stable thermal conductivity, and altered short-range-order development during heating.
Large nanoparticles or bulk-like systems have more stable thermal properties and less surface-induced disorder under the same heating conditions.
Interatomic-potential inaccuracies and short MD time scales may limit representation of long-term ordering kinetics and experimental surface effects.
The predicted magnitudes of size-dependent thermal conductivity and short-range-order evolution depend on the interatomic potential and simulation time scale.
Absence of a statistically significant size-dependent increase in disorder, decrease in thermal conductivity, or alteration of short-range order would falsify the hypothesis.
